title: Givvy — Spring Boot Item Exchange Platform
text:
A fully functional Spring Boot backend built with JPA, developed collaboratively as part of a Backend Programming course. Givvy is a community exchange platform that lets users create accounts, post items for donation, express interest in available items, and coordinate exchange appointments between donors and recipients.


I owned the features that drive the core exchange workflow:

Interest & offer matching — the logic allowing users to express interest in items and donors to offer items, forming the matches that power exchanges.
Dynamic appointment scheduling — a flexible system for coordinating exchange appointments between parties.
End-to-end testing — a thorough test suite covering these workflows from request to persistence, validating the full behavior of the features I built.

title: Mathematics Senior Capstone: Conjugacy and S-graph Shifts
text:
For my mathematics senior capstone, I studied conjugacy in symbolic dynamics, focusing on a class of shift spaces called \(\mathcal{S}\)-graph shifts. Conjugacy is a notion of equivalence between shifts that preserves their dynamical behavior, but it is difficult to establish, and a concrete result on conjugacy for \(\mathcal{S}\)-graph shifts remains an open problem.
In the paper, I work through a motivating example of two conjugate \(\mathcal{S}\)-graph shifts, examine a proposed (but unproven) tool called the core graph, and explore new ideas about disjoint cycle sets and Dillon’s entropy formula that suggest directions for future investigation.

title: Analyzing the DC BikeShare System
text:
Introduction
We are investigating the bike sharing data set, which includes data on the Capital Bikeshare System, a bike rental service in Washington D.C. The main variable of interest in this data set is count, which represents the total number of bikes rented in a given day (There is also hourly data available, though daily data is used for the purpose of this project). After setting up feature engineering, we build and analyze several models and utilize cross validation to evaluate and compare the models. Once the optimal model is chosen, it is then used on the test set and further evaluated for its performance.

title: Analyzing the DC BikeShare System
text:
Analysis/Methodology
We did some initial data exploration, looking in to the types of variables present, ranges of values for variables, any missing entries, etc. There were some variables we decided to remove from our dataset prior to model building for a number of reasons. For example, we removed the yr and date variables as these do not provide any helpful information for future predictions, and we would not want them influencing our model. We found no missing entries in the variables we will use. The only feature engineering we found it necessary to implement was normalizing numeric predictors and dummy encoding categorical predictors. We also created a minimal FE blueprint with no feature engineering to test applicable models on this as well. We considered an 80-20 split for splitting our data and creating training and test sets.
This is a supervised, regression problem so a logistic regression would not make sense to use in this case. Instead, we will build and compare the following models:

Linear Regression
KNN
Single Tree
Random Forest
Boosted Trees

All of these models besides KNN will be built on both the full feature engineered training data, as well as the minimal FE data. Minimal feature engineering only includes imputing missing values, and since we have none of those, the models will simply be trained and tested on the original training and test sets. All models will be trained and compared using the CV process to tune hyperparameters and obtain test predictions for accuracy.

# CV specifications

set.seed(208)

cv_specs_bike <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",    # CV method
                         number = 5,              # number of folds
                         repeats = 1)              # number of repeats


# for KNN

k_grid_bike <- expand.grid(k = seq(1, 51, by = 10))  


# for random forests

param_grid_rf_bike <- expand.grid(mtry = seq(1, 10, 1),    
                                   splitrule = "variance",
                                   min.node.size = 2)  


set.seed(208)

# linear (full FE)

                         data = bike_train,
                         method = "lm",
                         trControl = cv_specs_bike,
                         metric = "RMSE")

title: Analyzing the DC BikeShare System
text:
Conclusion
After performing cross validation to tune hyperparameters and compare training performance across all tested models, we found the optimal model to be the random forested implemented with minimal FE, and mtry=3. On the training set, this model yielded an RMSE of 1240 and RMSESD of 63. When training the final model, and using it to predict on our test set, we found an RMSE of around 1160.
When checking our VIP’s, we see the variables that influence our predictions the most are temperature, average temperature, and humidity. These may be expected. However, our model cannot give us any additional information about specifically how these variables influence prediction.
The random forest with minimal FE seems to be the optimal model on all accounts. Any others that are close to its performance would not add any additional interpretability, usefulness, or reduction in computation power. If we were looking for more interpretability or less resources used, we could perhaps train the linear model with no feature engineering. While this did perform outright worse than the random forest, its interpretability and minmimal computation power needed could make it useful in application.

title: Probability Experiment
text:
Experiment
Ingredients:

1 deck of 52 standard cards
4 six sided die, labeled a-d, with weights denoted by the following vectors

a -> equally weighted
b -> \(( 0.1,0.3,0.1,0.1,0.3,0.1 )\)
c -> \(( 0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.2 )\)
d -> \(( 0.15, 0.2, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 )\)

2 coins labeled 1 and 2 with the following probability p for heads

1 -> p = .75
2 -> p = .25


Instructions:

Shuffle the cards together to obtain a well mixed deck
Draw a card from the deck. Record the suit
For each suit:

If hearts, choose die a

If diamonds, choose die b

If spades, choose die c

If clubs, choose die d


Record which die you choose

If die a or c, grab coin 1
If die b or d, grab coin 2

Roll the die
Call the number on the face of the die N
Flip the coin you grabbed N times
Count the number of tails you get

Possible outcomes: \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\)


Analysis
Let us solve this problem directly. Define the random variable \(X\) = # of tails flipped. We can now use LOTP to find \(P(X=k)\) conditioning on which die we roll. So this will look like
\[\begin{eqnarray*}P(X=k) &=& P(X=k|\textrm{a})P(\textrm{a})+P(X=k|\textrm{b})P(\textrm{b})+P(X=k|\textrm{c})P(\textrm{c})+P(X=k|\textrm{d})P(\textrm{d})\\
&=& \frac{1}{4}\left(P(X=k|\textrm{a})+P(X=k|\textrm{b})+P(X=k|\textrm{c})+P(X=k|\textrm{d})\right)
\end{eqnarray*}\]
We know still that \(P(\textrm{a})=P(\textrm{b})=P(\textrm{c})=P(\textrm{d})=1/4\), as the die gets chosen by drawing a card from a shuffled deck of 52 cards, and looking at the suit with each suit equally likley. Let us now consider \(P(X=k|\textrm{a})\). In order to solve this for any of the terms in our LOTP we have here, we will again have to make use of the LOTP, this time conditioning on which number gets rolled on the die. So doing this we have,
\[
P(X=k|a)=\sum_{j=1}^6P(X=k|a,Rj)P(Rj|a).
\] Where \(Rj\) is the event of rolling the number \(j\) on the die. We can similarly write this for all of our conditional terms in our original LOTP.
\[
P(X=k|b)=\sum_{j=1}^6P(X=k|b,Rj)P(Rj|b).
\] \[
P(X=k|c)=\sum_{j=1}^6P(X=k|c,Rj)P(Rj|c).
\]
\[
P(X=k|d)=\sum_{j=1}^6P(X=k|d,Rj)P(Rj|d).
\]
Now note that in each case, the probability \(P(Rj|die)\) is given by the probability vectors of each respective die given at the beginning of the experiment. So we would like to calculate our probabilities \(P(X=k|a,Rj)\). Note that for any given die, we know which coin we have. For dies \(a\) and \(c\), we have coin one with probability \(p = .75\) of heads. For dies \(b\) and \(d\), we have coin two with probability \(p = .25\) of heads. So all the condition of which die we has does for our probability is tell us which coin we have. We are then just looking at \(P(X=k|Rj)\) which will be distributed \(Bin(1-p,j)\) for whatever \(p\) corresponds to the coin we are flipping. This is because we have a \(p\) coin, and we are flipping it \(j\) times, however we are counting the number of tails we get. So this is \(Bin(1-p,j)\). We can calculate all these probabilities for each coin and store them in a matrix.
For coin 1:

j = 1:6
px0 <- dbinom(0,j,.25)
px1 <- dbinom(1,j,.25)
px2 <- dbinom(2,j,.25)
px3 <- dbinom(3,j,.25)
px4 <- dbinom(4,j,.25)
px5 <- dbinom(5,j,.25)

So we now have two matrices denoting our probabilities \(P(X=k|\textrm{Rj})\) for coin 1, which corresponds to dices \(a\) and \(c\), and coin 2 which corresponds to dices \(b\) and \(d\). We can now use these matrices along with the vectors denoting the probabilities for each respective die to calculate the terms of our LOTP. Let us start with \(P(X=k|\textrm{a})\). Remember we have this written as,
\[
P(X=k|a)=\sum_{j=1}^6P(X=k|a,Rj)P(Rj|a).
\]
using the LOTP. Our values \(P(X=k|\textrm{a,Rj})\) are given by our matrix we’ve defined using the binomial for coin 1 (the coin corresponding to die \(a\)). Our values \(P(Rj|a)\) are given by the probability vector of die \(a\), which is uniform. Note that for the \(k=0\) case, we would want to take the dot product of our probability vector for die \(a\), and the first row of our matrix for coin 1. So in general, the solution for all \(k\) in the support here will be the dot product of our probability vector for our die, and each row in our matrix. We must transpose the matrix as we want the dot product with each row, but when you dot a vector and a matrix is dots the vector with each column. So transposing the matrix will allow us to dot the vector and the matrix itself to calculate all our desired probabilities at once. Let’s do this.

We can now begin to compute the dot products. Again, we are starting with \(P(X=k|\textrm{a})\).
Start by defining the probability vector for the die \(a\), then take the dot product with our transpose matrix for coin 1. This will be equal to our LOTP for all \(k\) in the support.

So we can see for example that \(P(X=0|a)=.411\), and so on.
We can now repeat this for all of our LOTP conditioning on which die we roll. Moving on to \(P(X=k|b)\). For die \(b\), we choose coin two. So for \(P(X=k|b)\) we will dot the probability vector for the die with the matrix for coin 2. Start with the probability vector for \(b\).

Define the probability vector for die \(c\), and dot with the coin 1 transpose matrix.

And finally for \(P(X=k|d)\) which corresponds to coin 2.
Again start with defining the probability vector for die \(d\), then taking the dot with the transpose of the coin 2 matrix.

Now that we have all of these, we can go back to our original LOTP we started with, which is
\[\begin{eqnarray*}P(X=k) &=& P(X=k|\textrm{a})P(\textrm{a})+P(X=k|\textrm{b})P(\textrm{b})+P(X=k|\textrm{c})P(\textrm{c})+P(X=k|\textrm{d})P(\textrm{d})\\
&=& \frac{1}{4}\left(P(X=k|\textrm{a})+P(X=k|\textrm{b})+P(X=k|\textrm{c})+P(X=k|\textrm{d})\right)
\end{eqnarray*}\]
We have all of our terms \(P(X=k|\textrm{die})\) for all dice \(a\)-\(d\) defined in our vectors we found with the dot product. We can now just take the vector sum of all of our vectors corresponding to \(P(X=k|\textrm{die})\), multiply by the constant 1/4, and we will have a vector of length seven denoting the probability of flipping 0-6 tails. In other words, we will have the value of the PMF for all \(k\) in our support stored in this vector.

PMF <-1/4*c(pxka+pxkb+pxkc+pxkd)  #Making use of the c to turn this back in to a vector data type.

sum(PMF)

[1] 1


Looks like this is a valid PMF. Nice! We can also plot this.

plot(PMF)








Cool!
Also, let us note that the indexing our PMF vector, and subsequently our PMF plot, are off by one. This is due to the 1-based indexing in r, even though our first entry in our vector corresponds to the \(k=0\) case. So, for example the probability of getting 4 tails is

Simulation
Now let us simulate our experiment to see if it matches our calculated PMF.
First, I will create some structures corresponding to my ingredients in R:

coin1 <- 0.75
coin2 <- 0.25
die_a <- c(1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6)
die_b <- c(0.1,0.3,0.1,0.1,0.3,0.1)
die_c <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.2)
die_d <- c(0.15, 0.2, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)

Now I write a function that will run the experiment:

Trials <- 10^4  # number of times to run the experiment; start with a small number for debugging
simulate <- function() { # each call to simulate is one trial
  die = c(0,0,0,0,0,0) #Create an empty vector defining our die to manipulate later
  
  N = (sample(1:4,1,replace=FALSE)) #Sample a random number from 1 to 4 to simulate getting 
                                    #one of the four suits from drawing a card
  
  #Assign die and coin accordingly based on card draw
  if(N == 1) { 
    die = die_a
    coin = coin1;
    }
  
  if(N == 2) {                
    die = die_b
    coin = coin2
    }
  
  if(N == 3) {
    die = die_c
    coin = coin1;
    }
  
  if(N == 4) {
    die = die_d
    coin = coin2
    }
  
  N = (sample(1:6,1,replace=FALSE,die)) # roll die
  #Loop through simulating coin flips based on the die roll. Count hte tails
  tails = 0
  for(i in 1:N) {      
    if(runif(1)>coin) { 
      tails = tails+1
    }
  }
  return(tails)
}
r <- replicate(Trials,simulate())  # run experiment many times and store outcomes in a vector


percentages <- table(r)/Trials  # tabulate frequencies of outcomes

title: A Layered Grammar of Graphics Paper Review
text:
The fifth and final project of CMSC405 involved reading, analyzing, and presenting on a Data Science paper that is foundational in the growing field. My partner Laura Henze and I chose the paper A Layered Grammar of Graphics written by Hadley Wickham. This paper lays the theoretical foundation for the highly influential R data visualization package ggplot2. We created both a poster presentation, as well as two individual critical analyses of this paper. Find below our poster, as well as my personal critical analysis.


  



Open the poster full screen in a new tab

A Layered Grammar of Graphics Summary and Critical Analysis
The title of this paper is A Layered Grammar of Graphics written by Hadley Wickham. The central goal of Wickham in this paper was to formalize and streamline the way we produce statistical graphics digitally. This was, and continues to be, a very significant concept as people from a variety of different fields make use of software to visualize data. Having a widely recognized, and easy to use framework that can be applied to create many different kinds of graphics will serve a very large population. An earlier paper by Leland Wilkinson laid the groundwork which Wickham built off. Wilkinson proposed a “Grammar of Graphics” that broke digital graphics in to a set of building blocks, all of which were orthogonal and could be edited individually to create a graphic. This visualization framework was then implemented in its own programming language. While useful, and possibly capable of describing a wider range of graphics than Wickham’s, Wilkinson’s framework was overall verbose. It gets messy quickly and requires a lot of explicit coding to set things up. Wickham sought to not only simplify this approach, but also embed his own framework directly into an already widely used programming language - R, with the package ggplot2.
Wickham took the idea of Wilkinson’s grammar, modified it slightly, and expanded upon it to create his proposed layered grammar of graphics. This came with a similar set of building blocks, all of which could be modified individually to create various kinds of plots. Perhaps the most foundational piece of the proposed framework was the layers. Wickham’s grammar consists of 7 main components. Data, aesthetic mappings, geometric objects, statistical transformations, scales, coordinate systems, and facets. Of these, the coordinate system, scales, and facets all act on the overall graphic as a whole. Data, aesthetic mappings, geometric objects, and statistical transformations comprise each layer. Under the pretense of this grammar, every graphic is built up of one or more layers, along with the necessary scales (while these correspond to the aesthetic mappings in each layer, but are still considered to be part of the overall graphic), coordinate system, and faceting. The exception here is one may propose default data, and aesthetic mappings which get applied to the entire plot as a whole, becoming the data and aesthetics for each layer. The grammar defined this way provides a framework for producing a wide variety of graphics. However, when implementing it in this base form we see some similar issues to that of Wilkinson’s. That is, it is very verbose and requires a lot of code, making learning and reading the syntax more complicated. To remedy this, Wickham also proposed a hierarchy of defaults. Several of the most commonly used plots, such as a scatter plot or a bar plot, can be created using ggplot2 only specifying data, aesthetics, and the geometric object. The rest (scales, stats, etc) gets filled in using Wickham’s system of defaults. This leads to simpler, and easier to learn code for widely used plots, while still maintaining the level of precision and control with the ability to override any default. This allows for a low level of entry (a biologist with minimal coding experience can easily make a plot) while also maintaining a high ceiling (a well versed coder can make creative and unique plots by explicitly defining each component). This system makes Wickham’s grammar, implemented in ggplot2, extremely powerful for a wide range of graphics and users. Additionally, it certainly proves to be a general simplification of the grammar proposed by Wilkinson.
There are certainly some limitations to this grammar, some of which are acknowledged by Wickham himself in the paper. One limitation comes in the creation of area plots, such as bar charts or histograms. He states how these can be constructed using the grammar, but there is not a lot of insight into their underlying structure. This makes it difficult to create/understand useful variations. He proposes it might be useful to define “subgrammars” for different families of plots, allowing for more specific control over them. Wickham also mentions how this proposed system does not tell us how to display anything besides a dataframe. So things such as clusterings or classifications become a lot more complex. Another limitation of the base implementation is the lack of interactability. As it stood there was no way to incorporate user interactability into a ggplot2 graphic, which is desirable in many contexts. This proved to be a big gap when it came to actual usability across a wide range of fields. However there are many extensions that add on to ggplot2, several of which provides interactability. In fact all of these issues mentioned may be tackled by other users adding extentions. This idea of extensions filling the gaps may be seen as both a limitation, or a strength. For one, it is a limitation as many of these desirable functionalities require an extra extension. On the other hand, the ability to add extensions (or edit the package ggplot2 itself) provides a clear and definitive way to fill any gaps one may see in this implementation. Another limitation of the framework is the complexity. Despite the fact that it does certainly simplify things overall, and provides a concrete framework for creating graphics, there is still a learning curve. This gets especially steep when looking to create increasingly complex graphics. Some of the abstract concepts present in the framework may be difficult to beginners, and this holds especially true as you look in to editing each component manually. Overall though these limitations have not effected the real world applicability and usability of ggplot2 and the layered grammar of graphics. There is sufficient documentation and instruction for most users to understand the basics. Additionally, a lot of the limitations only show up when executing high complexity use cases for this package. The large majority of users are using ggplot2 for creating relatively well understood graphics, and one may argue that this was the primary goal for this package. If looking through that lens, the ideas from this paper implemented in ggplot2 performed very well and is still extremely useful across several scenarios despite some existing limitations.
The primary, and certainly most notable influence of this paper was the frameworks implementation in the R package ggplot2. This package completely changed the world of creating statistical graphics digitally. It is one of, if not the most widely use graphics software in both the world of data science, and beyond. It is used by people from pretty much any field one could imagine that involves data/data analysis. This makes the ideas proposed in this paper arguably some of the most substantial in recent history for the field of data science. It has also inspired the creation of several other packages and add ons to ggplot2, implementing extra features such as interactability mentioned above. The ideas proposed have also became the framework for data visualizations outside of R as well, with examples existing in Python, Matlab, and more.
My biggest conceptual takeaway really has to do with how much is happening behind the scenes with ggplot2. In particular, something I found really insightful was the hierarchy of defaults Wickham implemented. The idea of having a modular system for creating graphics, with ever component being editable creates a very powerful system. However, at face value it also creates a very complex system for a beginner user to learn. I can imagine trying to learn all the specific lines of code for each component being very difficult even for just a basic plot. Let alone memorizing all the different combinations to be able to use them in an efficient manner while working on a large project. I find the idea of implementing smart defaults based on the most widely used applications for various plots very smart. I imagine that this package would be nowhere near what it is now without this implementation of defaults. In fact, reading about this implementation made me realize something important about the design of data science tools. That is, a developer must consider who may be using their tools, and how to best suit their needs. Here Wickham is presumably developing for a very large user base. As such, there will be many novice users. This requires tools that are relatively easy to learn how to use. With the system of defaults, most novice coders can easily learn to make a large family of plots. On the flipside however, Wickham has also catered to the other side of his user base. Very experienced coders and data scientists may dive deep in to the component wise control of this grammar to create complex visualizations. This idea of providing tools that suit the needs of users across all skill levels seems to me to be a key aspect of creating a widely used tool in the world of data science. I would say this idea in and of itself connects largely to specifically my developing journey at Lawrence, and being very user conscious when creating tools, and products. I really like the idea of creating tools that are have low barrier to entry but high levels of complexity when diving deep. I will carry this idea forward in my career.

title: Computer Science Senior Capstone
text:
For my computer science senior capstone, I begun working on a small business with two partners, one being my good friend Aaron Stathopoylos. We have one partner focused on the business end, while me and Aaron have been developing our product. This product is called DEMS. The goal is to build a comprehensive system for dental offices to track and manage all their equipment and equipment maintenance, from purchase through its entire lifecycle. This is currently a massive hole in the dental industry. We hope to deploy in the next several months. We do not have a live demo yet, so this page will showcase a few screenshots and explanations of features. Check back in the near future to get access to a live demo!

Admin Dashboard

Office Dahsboard

Maintain Admin and Office accounts for clean management of single branches to chains of clinics
Record and maintain comprehensive list of equipment for each office, including all pertinent details such as maintenace requirements, warranty information, neccessary parts, etc.
Record and maintain comprehensive list of all pending, scheduled, and completed maintenance appointments
Automated maintenance appointment scheduling. Simply record your top 2 or 3 maintenance companies, along with their contact information as a part of your office profile. Then with a simple click of a button you can send a generated email requesting a maintenance appointment for a specific piece of equipment. This cuts out on manually scheduling, allowing it to happen all in one place.
AI Assistant to automate tedious data entry

The goal here is to save time, and increase productivity by providing a simple and organized one stop shop for all dental equipment tracking needs.

title: Tristan Zook
text: To many, Lego sets are merely a plaything for children. However, as with many “toy” items there is an avid community of adult Lego enjoyers. Whether this is purely to build, or to collect a wide variety of sets, there are plenty of people around the world interested in purchasing Lego sets. And with buyers, there are sellers. Many recognize this demand for Legos, and are in the market for buying and reselling. One platform that is often used for individuals to sell Lego sets to others is Amazon. We have access to a large dataset of various Lego sets, containing a variety of information, including listed Amazon prices for these sets. In this report, we will be attempting to build a model that predicts a Lego sets Amazon price based on specific factors about the Lego set. Or at least to understand how each factor of a lego set may contribute to its value. This could be helpful for any and all who are looking to resell Lego sets, whether they are seasoned or first time sellers. In building our model, we will be ignoring the original listed price for each set, imagining that we as resellers will not have this information when attempting to sell a Lego set. We can then compare our final model to a model using only the original listed price (assuming this should be the strongest indication of Amazon price) to see how well are developed model works.

title: Tristan Zook
text:
Results
The first model we built had very apparent issues, discussed as the quadratic relationship present in the residual plot. As such, we will focus more on the models built afterwards. Our first was a model predicting log price using pieces and pieces squared. Here we see a moderately high \(R^2\) value, with 0.58. So this tells us that approximately 58% of the variability is explained with this model. It is difficult to obtain a meaningful interpretation of the coefficients here as this is a quadratic model. The interpretation of our intercept term is nonsensical, being that it would apply to a Lego set with no pieces. However, we can use the coefficients on our pieces terms to obtain an estimation on when the price will peak based on the number of pieces. Seeing as our coefficients on our quadratic term is negative, we know this will happen. log(price), and therefore price will peak at \(-b/2a = -2.033e-03/(2*-3.105e-07) = 3273.752\). So essentially this tells us that after around 3200 pieces, the price of sets will start to decrease rather than increase. This may suggest that at a certain point, larger Lego sets become more of a hassle or nuisance to build, so people won’t want to pay as much. We see essentially zero p-values on all of our terms here. This suggests that pieces, and pieces squared, both have statistically discernible relationships with Amazon price.
We now move forward to our next model, which adds unique_pieces on to our previous model. Despite concerns with multicollinearity, we maintain ~0 p-values for all of our terms in this model. The exponentiated value of our unique_pieces term is 1.0027439. This tells us that our model predicts on average a 1.0027439 times increase in price for each additional unique piece in the set, as compared to adding an additional regular piece. In other words, a roughly .3 percent increase in price per unique_piece vs a regular piece. A 95% confidence interval tells us that we are 95% confident that this increase will be in the range from .2 to .35 percent increase per additional unique piece on average. As mentioned, we have essentially a zero p-value on this coefficient, though it is slightly higher than those of the pieces terms. This low p-value does suggest evidence that there is a statistically discernible relationship between unique_pieces and Amazon price. We also saw, when performing an F-test between this and the previous model, that we obtain an F-statistic of 63 with an essentially 0 p-values. This is a moderately high F-statistic, with the low p-value supporting that there is a statistically discernible difference. All this suggests that this model is an improvement on our previous one. Taking a look at our R^2, we see a jump to 0.6174. So around 61% of our variability is explained. This is not a large jump. However, it is still an improvement overall. All this seems to be a good sign for this model.
Our final model attempts to add the categorical theme as a predictor of our Amazon price. Right away, we see an \(R^2\) value of 0.6455, indicating that around 64.5% of variability is explained by this model. This is about the same sized jump as we made from our first model to our second. However, this time it comes at the cost of quite a bit more complexity. Additionally, looking at our F-tests, we get an F-stat of 21 for comparing this model and our first model, and 11 comparing this model and our second model. Both of these F-statistics have low p-values, suggesting that this is a statistically discernible difference. However, these F-values are not super high, and certainly lower than that of the second model compared to the first. In fact, we see that when comparing to just the first model, the second model made more of an improvement (based on the F test) than this third model does, despite the fact that this model still contains unique pieces. This is indication that this model may not be the best, especially given its complexity. There is still more to conclude from this model though. The coefficients for pieces, pieces^2, and unique pieces all still have essentially 0 p-values. So we still see strong evidence that these are meaningful terms. Two of the theme coefficients however have very large p-values, suggesting that these are not meaningful terms, and whether or not the set has this theme is not an important predictor compared to the number of pieces/unique pieces. However, three of our terms - Classic & Creative Building, Fantasy & Adventure, and Specialty & Collectible Themes all have p-values below .05. Thus we have strong evidence that a Lego set being of one of these themes does actually influence the price. The exponentiated coefficients on these are 0.7042700, 0.7995849, 0.6711235 respectively. So our model expects on average a 30%, 20%, and 33% average decrease in price respectively if the Lego set is any of these themes, holding the number of pieces and unique pieces constant. Taking a look at the confidence intervals for each of these, we see a lot of variation. For a specific example, we are 95% confident that the average decrease in estimated price (holding pieces and unique pieces constant) if a set is a specialty and collectible theme is between 48% and 15%. This is a very large range. The other three themes listed also show a similarly wide range, though this is the most extreme. All this seems to tell us that a few of these themes do matter, however we are not very certain of how much. There is a lot of variability/uncertainty here. Another thing to consider, is that it seems we’ve only obtained statistically discernible results for themes that decrease price, which may not be of much interest to a collector or a seller.

title: Tristan Zook
text:
Conclusion
We built three main models attempting to predict Amazon price based on features of a Lego set. You as a collector, or seller, may be interested in knowing what sort of price you could put on a Lego set you have based on its features. The goal here was to build a model that does not use any information about the listed price of the Lego set to see if it was possible to ascertain resale value from just a Lego set itself. The three models we built were a quadratic model on the number of pieces, then a model adding the number of unique pieces to this, then a model adding what theme the Lego set was. The final model using theme group is not one I believe we should consider. For one, we did not see a large increase in R^2 considering the increased complexity of the model. Additionally, several of the coefficients proved to be not meaningful based on the p-values, and the ones that were had a lot of variability based on confidence intervals. Furthermore, these coefficients that were discernible do not seem to add good information for the context of reselling, especially considering yet again the complexity. There are also some obvious limitations to this model. The six theme groups used were developed by chat-gpt. I sent the list of all themes from the dataset to chat-gpt, and requested that chat-gpt break them in to six categories for me. This is possibly unreliable, and may not capture something important could easily be missed. Additionally, the size of these groups were uneven which can skew p-values and increase variability. So based on all this I’d like to turn my attention to the first two models. Between the first and the second, we again only see a small increase in R^2, from 58% to 61% variability explained. However this time we see a much larger F-statistic when comparing the two, suggesting a more significant difference. We are also adding less complexity with this change compared to the third model, thus getting the same level of increase in \(R^2\) for less cost. Both models see all coefficients as statistically discernible and meaningful. All these things seem to point to model 2 being the best choice. Clearly unique_pieces does seem to influence the price. However, a counterargument against model 2 could be made. When considering the practicality, we do see unique_pieces making a very small impact, even though it is statistically discernible. With 95% confidence that price will increase by .2% to .35% per unique_piece, this does seem to be a very small impact. Especially if we consider that most sets do not have a large amount of these kinds of pieces. With this being said, for the few sets that do have a large amount of unique_pieces, this will still prove to be a large difference. So seeing as this does not add a lot of additional complexity, and clearly suggests that unique_pieces has a statistically discernible relationship with Amazon price, it seems that this second model is the ideal one.
This model being the best one aligns with my expectations based on data exploration. I knew that pieces and unique_pieces would likely turn out to be the strongest and most meaningful predictors. I was slightly worried about multicollinearity, and equally as surprised when this did not seem to be much of an issue at all. I was hopeful about the theme group being a meaningful predictor, however I am not surprised that it did not seem to be as such. The variability between themes was not extremely pronounced in data exploration, though it was present. And the additional factor of the chat-gpt generated groups brings in an entire new dimension of unreliability.
Turning my attention now to the original goal. How well can we predict Amazon price based on Lego set features, without using original listed price. The model we created using only price to directly predicted Amazon price saw an R^2 value of .79, so approximately 80% of variability was explained. The model we decided on as our most meaningful, model 2, only explained around 61% of the variability. So we clearly were not able to get nearly as close with these factors alone as with the listed price. This is to be expected, as one can imagine that the listed price is usually what is being put as the Amazon price on average. Another thing to consider is as follows - for this specific question, in the context of reselling as a Lego collector, this dataset may not be very accurate. I am unclear where this data comes from, and the Amazon prices are most likely largely depictions of people directly selling a set based on its original price. Factors contributing to how much collectors will pay for a set may not be reflected in this dataset. A more curated and careful dataset would likely have to be generated to get a more accurate idea for this specific question. However, if you are stuck looking to resell or find the value on a Lego set without knowing the original listed price, the models we’ve built here can serve as a good guide for what factors are the most influential in determining the Amazon price.

title: Mighty Big Problem — Simulating the Perihelion Precession of Mercury
text:
A numerical simulation that reproduces the anomalous precession of Mercury’s perihelion — including the famous ~43 arcseconds/century that Newtonian gravity can’t explain and general relativity can. Written in Python with NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib.
For the full derivation — the equations of motion, the initial conditions, the relativistic correction term, and the benchmark formulas the results are checked against — see the accompanying writeup in this repo.



The orbit of a single planet around a single star, under Newton’s inverse-square law, is a perfectly closed ellipse — it never precesses. Yet Mercury’s orbit does, at roughly 575 arcseconds per century (after removing the much larger apparent precession from the drifting equinox). Explaining that residual was a genuine crisis in physics, and its resolution became one of the first triumphs of general relativity.
This project rebuilds the answer from scratch, one effect at a time:

Part A — Two-body baseline. Mercury and the Sun alone. The exact answer is zero precession, so this run measures the numerical noise floor of the method (~−23″/century here) — a sanity check rather than a physical result.
Part B — Newtonian planetary perturbations. Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, Earth, and Mars are added one by one. Their combined gravitational tugging precesses Mercury’s orbit by about 530″/century (accepted value ≈ 532″).
Part C — General relativity. A single relativistic correction term is added to the Sun’s pull on Mercury, closing the remaining gap and taking the total to about 576″/century — a GR contribution of ~46″/century against the textbook 43″.

Each stage numerically integrates the equations of motion with scipy.odeint, extracts the perihelion (closest point to the Sun) on every orbit, converts those points to angular positions, and fits a line whose slope is the precession rate.

title: Mighty Big Problem — Simulating the Perihelion Precession of Mercury
text:
The orbit of a single planet around a single star, under Newton’s inverse-square law, is a perfectly closed ellipse — it never precesses. Yet Mercury’s orbit does, at roughly 575 arcseconds per century (after removing the much larger apparent precession from the drifting equinox). Explaining that residual was a genuine crisis in physics, and its resolution became one of the first triumphs of general relativity.
This project rebuilds the answer from scratch, one effect at a time:

Part A — Two-body baseline. Mercury and the Sun alone. The exact answer is zero precession, so this run measures the numerical noise floor of the method (~−23″/century here) — a sanity check rather than a physical result.
Part B — Newtonian planetary perturbations. Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, Earth, and Mars are added one by one. Their combined gravitational tugging precesses Mercury’s orbit by about 530″/century (accepted value ≈ 532″).
Part C — General relativity. A single relativistic correction term is added to the Sun’s pull on Mercury, closing the remaining gap and taking the total to about 576″/century — a GR contribution of ~46″/century against the textbook 43″.

Each stage numerically integrates the equations of motion with scipy.odeint, extracts the perihelion (closest point to the Sun) on every orbit, converts those points to angular positions, and fits a line whose slope is the precession rate.

This is the plain-language report that accompanies the technical analysis of the DC BikeShare data.

title: Analysis of BikeShare Program
text:
Overview
We trained multiple types of machine learning models to predict the number of bikes rented each day through the Capital BikeShare program in D.C. The data contained several variables influencing predictions of bike count, including features like wind speed and temperature, as well as information on the month, season, and whether it was a working day or holiday. Our final model can be used to inform you of how to proceed in the planning/implementation of bike share programs across the city.

title: Analysis of BikeShare Program
text:
How Accurate Is the Model?
We found the optimal model to be what we call a random forest applied directly to the raw dataset. When testing our model, we found it can make predictions within around 1160 bikes rented for any given day. When taking into account the stability of our model during training, we could perhaps expect this variability to be more around 1100 to 1200 off the true count when making predictions. What this variability really means is that when predicting, we can expect to either over- or underestimate the true count by a value within this reported margin.
With this information, you can make an estimate about how many bikes to put out/have available on any given day. We may suggest having around 500 more than what our model may predict for a given day, as it is possible that our model may underestimate. However, considering available resources, having an additional 1000 bikes may not be feasible.

title: Analysis of BikeShare Program
text:
What Drives Bike Rentals?
I am sure you may also be interested in any specific factors that might indicate when more people are more likely to rent bikes. For example, how can we expect the count to change on a weekday versus a weekend? Unfortunately, our model does a poor job of telling us such specific correlations.
We can determine the features that seem to influence the predicted count of bikes rented the most. These were:

the temperature
the average temperature
the humidity

However, using our model, we cannot determine how directly these features influence our prediction. Rather, just that they influence them in some way. In the case of some features, we may be able to ascertain their influence by thinking about it. It makes sense that more people may wish to rent bikes when it is warm out, for example. However, even with these qualitative guesses, we may be missing information. For example, if it is too hot, maybe fewer people will rent bikes.
Furthermore, there are some features that may have impacts we cannot qualitatively predict. For example, how things such as weekday vs weekend, holiday, or the weather (not temperature directly, more like sunny or cloudy) can impact our count.

title: Analysis of BikeShare Program
text:
A More Interpretable Alternative
This is the downside of our model. If you are interested in a model that can better tell us these things, we have also tested out a linear model, which is much more interpretable. With this, we can see directly how each predictor is correlated with the count prediction. However, in training, this model was consistently more unstable with higher prediction error. So it will be more inaccurate. If this is something you are interested in, please let us know.
This concludes our report. Let us know if there are any questions.
